title: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
summary: Prompting an LLM to grade query-document relevance, measuring agreement with kappa and alpha, checking system rankings with Kendall's tau, and the biases and circularity traps that make human gold labels essential.
outcomes: Explain how Bing and UMBRELA structure a relevance judging prompt and which prompt features changed agreement
Compute a confusion matrix, Cohen's kappa, weighted kappa and Krippendorff's alpha for human versus LLM labels
Compute Kendall's tau between system rankings under human and LLM labels and explain why it can be high when kappa is modest
Detect and mitigate position, verbosity and self-preference bias, including swap-and-tie pairwise judging
Explain circularity when a judge is also a ranking component and design a gold-set based validation process

lessons.title: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation

blocks.md:
From the ranking metrics course you can compute NDCG@10 for a ranked list, but only if every returned document has a **relevance label**: a grade saying how useful that document is for that query. In TREC terms the set of labels is called the **qrels** (query relevance judgments).

Labels are the expensive part. Every new system returns some documents nobody has judged yet, every new query needs fresh judgments, and a search team wants to compare dozens of variants per week.

This course uses the four-grade scale of the TREC Deep Learning and TREC 2024 RAG tracks:

- **0 Non-relevant**: the passage has nothing to do with the query.
- **1 Related**: related to the query but contains no part of an answer.
- **2 Highly relevant**: contains a partial or complete answer, but it may be unclear or hidden among extraneous text.
- **3 Perfectly relevant**: dedicated to the query and contains an answer.

An **LLM judge** (or LLM assessor) is a large language model prompted with the query, the passage and these definitions, asked to output one grade.

blocks.title: Where labels enter an offline evaluation

nodes.label:
Pool: top-k docs
from every system

scenes.caption: Classic Cranfield-style evaluation: every system runs every query, the top results are pooled, and humans grade the pool.
The human step is slow and costly, and labels from third-party assessors can still disagree with what the real searcher wanted.
The LLM judge replaces (or assists) the human step: same pool, same grade scale, minutes instead of days.
The judge is only trusted after it is checked against a small, carefully built gold set of human labels. This validation loop is the core of the method.
Labels feed metrics, metrics feed the leaderboard. A judge is good if the leaderboard it produces matches the one humans would produce.

blocks.md: Thomas, Spielman, Craswell and Mitra (SIGIR 2024) describe how Bing does this. They collect a modest set of **gold labels** from real searchers who had the need and gave careful feedback, then choose the LLM and prompt whose labels agree best with that gold set. The chosen judge then labels at scale. They state that Bing has used LLMs, together with expert human labellers, for most of its offline metrics since late 2022.

Their internal comparison (their Table 4, relative to a typical crowd worker) reports the LLM as the most accurate labeller against searcher gold (+28 percent, versus +24 percent for employees and +19 percent for the best crowd workers), with about 10 times the throughput and about 1/20 of the cost. The authors stress these figures depend on Bing's own contracts and training.

Academic evaluations came to similar conclusions. Faggioli et al. (2023) reported about USD 0.01 per GPT-3.5 judgment, compared with USD 0.25 per human judgment reported earlier for a task of similar scope.

An LLM judge does not remove the need for humans. Both Bing and the TREC studies check the judge against human labels, and Bing re-labels a stratified weekly sample with trained assessors to catch drift. Without a gold set you cannot tell whether the judge is right.
LLM-as-judge for relevance is a measurement instrument. Like any instrument, you calibrate it against a trusted reference (human gold labels) before you read numbers off it.

blocks.question: A team has 2,000 queries and 40 ranker variants per week, and wants NDCG@10 for all of them. What is the main reason they consider an LLM judge?
options: NDCG cannot be computed from human labels
Each new variant surfaces unjudged documents, and human labels for all of them are too slow and costly
LLM labels are always more accurate than human labels
LLMs can compute NDCG directly without labels
blocks.explain: NDCG needs a grade for every returned document. New rankers keep surfacing unjudged documents, so the labelling bill grows with every experiment. The LLM judge makes that bill small. Accuracy is not automatic: it has to be checked against gold labels.

blocks.question: Bing selects its judge prompt by agreement with which reference?
options: Labels from typical crowd workers
The judge's own labels from a previous week
Careful feedback from real searchers who had the information need
Click-through rate on the live search page
blocks.explain: Thomas et al. use first-party gold labels from searchers who had the need, because third-party labellers (crowd or staff) can systematically misread intent. Agreement with crowd labels would only reproduce the crowd's mistakes.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a relevance judging prompt

blocks.md:
A judge prompt is a labelling guideline written for a model instead of a person. The Bing prompt (Thomas et al., Figure 2) has four parts:

1. **Instructions**: the grade scale, adapted from the TREC assessor instructions, optionally with a **role** line ("You are a search quality rater evaluating the relevance of web pages").
2. **The pair**: the query, optionally the TREC **description** and **narrative** that spell out the information need, then the document text between markers.
3. **Step-by-step instructions**: consider the intent, then optionally rate **aspects** (match to intent M, trustworthiness T) before an overall score O; optionally simulate **multiple** judges.
4. **Output format**: a JSON snippet so the answer parses.

blocks.title: The Bing prompt, part by part

nodes.label:
Steps: intent, then
M and T aspects (A)

scenes.caption: Always present: the grade scale, the query, the document, and an output format. Grey boxes are the five optional features Bing switched on and off, giving 32 prompt variants.
Role (R): "you are a search quality rater". Averaged over the other features it lowered kappa by 0.04.
Description (D) and narrative (N) give the assessor's statement of what the query means. D added 0.01 kappa, N added 0.06.
Aspects (A): rate match to intent and trustworthiness before the overall score. The biggest single gain, +0.21 kappa, likely from the step-by-step structure.
Multiple judges (M): ask one call to simulate five raters and average. It hurt, -0.13 kappa on average. Effects were not additive across features.
Best variant on TREC Robust: D, N and A on ("-DNA-"), kappa 0.64 against the TREC assessors on binarised labels.

blocks.md: **Cohen's kappa** (defined precisely in the next lesson) measures agreement corrected for chance: 1 is perfect, 0 is chance level. Thomas et al. ran GPT-4 at temperature 0 on a stratified sample of 3,000 TREC Robust 2004 query-document pairs, scored with 0 to 2 grades and binarised for comparison. Across the 32 variants kappa ranged from 0.20 to 0.64. For scale: two groups of trained TREC assessors agree at about kappa 0.52 (computed from Cormack et al.), so the best prompts are at human level.

blocks.title: Average effect of each prompt feature on kappa (Bing, Table 2)

scenes.caption: Effect of switching each feature on, averaged over the settings of the others. Bar height is the size of the effect; red bars lowered kappa.
The two features people often add by habit, a persona and a panel of simulated judges, both hurt here. Aspects (+0.21) was by far the largest single effect.

blocks.prompt: Thomas et al. then kept the best design (-DNA-) fixed and only reworded the instructions, writing 42 paraphrases with the same meaning. How far do you expect kappa to move?
blocks.reveal:
A lot: mean kappa across paraphrases ranged from **0.50 to 0.72**, and it was not obvious from the text which wording would win. One paraphrase ("0 = no match, 1 = some match, 2 = great match ...") scored 0.72 versus 0.64 for the original.

The good news from their repeated 1500/1500 splits: picking the best variant on one half almost always still beat the baseline on the other half (989 of 1000 splits for paraphrases). So tuning wording against a gold set is low-regret, but any single prompt's number is one sample from a wide range.

blocks.md: UMBRELA (Upadhyay et al., 2024) is an open-source reproduction of the Bing assessor. It adapts the -DNA- design to the 0 to 3 TREC DL scale, runs GPT-4o at temperature 0, and asks for a single line `##final score: N`. The prompt below is the version used for the TREC 2024 RAG track (Upadhyay et al., Figure 2), wrapped in a minimal parser.

blocks.code:
PROMPT = '''Given a query and a passage, you must provide a score on an
integer scale of 0 to 3 with the following meaning:
0 = represent that the passage has nothing to do with the query,
1 = represents that the passage seems related to the query but does
not contain any part of an answer to it,
2 = represents that the passage contains a partial or complete answer
for the query, but the answer may be a bit unclear, or hidden amongst
extraneous information and
3 = represents that the passage is dedicated to the query and contains
a partial or complete answer to it.
Query: {query}
Passage: {passage}
Split this problem into steps:
Consider the underlying intent of the search.
Measure how well the content matches a likely intent of the query (M).
Measure how trustworthy the passage is (T).
Consider the aspects above and the relative importance of each, and
decide on a final score (O). Final score must be an integer value only.
Do not provide any code in result. Provide each score in the format of:
##final score: score without providing any reasoning.'''

import re

def judge(llm, query, passage):
    out = llm(PROMPT.format(query=query, passage=passage), temperature=0)
    m = re.search(r"##final score:\s*([0-3])", out)
    return int(m.group(1)) if m else None   # unparseable: drop, do not guess
blocks.caption: The UMBRELA prompt as printed in the TREC 2024 RAG study, plus a parser. The llm callable stands for your model client. Bing dropped unparseable outputs (90 of 96,000) rather than guessing.

blocks.md: Treat the prompt like a labelling guideline under version control: fix the overall design first (scale, aspects, output format), then explore wording against the gold set, and re-validate whenever you change the model, the prompt or the document format.

blocks.question: You add "You are an expert search quality rater. Ask five independent raters and average their scores" to a working judge prompt. Based on Bing's ablation, what should you expect?
options: A large gain, because personas and ensembles always help
No change, because the model ignores framing
Better agreement, but only on long documents
Possibly worse agreement: role and multiple judges each lowered kappa on average, so measure before adopting
blocks.explain: In Table 2 of Thomas et al., the role line averaged -0.04 kappa and simulated multiple judges -0.13. Effects interact (the paper notes they are not additive), which is exactly why every prompt change has to be measured against gold labels rather than assumed.

blocks.question: Which prompt feature gave the largest average improvement in Bing's TREC Robust experiments?
options: Asking for aspect scores (match to intent, trustworthiness) before the overall score
Including the TREC description field
Adding the role statement
Asking for five simulated judges
blocks.explain: Aspects added +0.21 kappa on average. The authors suggest the step-by-step structure, not the particular aspects, is what helps; Bing uses several aspects in production.

lessons.title: Measuring judge agreement: confusion matrix and Cohen's kappa

blocks.md: Before trusting a judge, compare it with humans on the same pairs. Our toy has 3 queries with 4 candidate documents each, 12 query-document pairs, labelled by a human and by an LLM judge on the 0 to 3 scale. The numbers are invented for teaching, but the pattern (the LLM is a bit more lenient) is the one the TREC 2024 RAG study reports.

scenes.caption: Each column is one query-document pair. q1 is "how long do cats sleep", q2 "vitamin d deficiency symptoms", q3 "python sort list of dicts by key".
Exact matches in green: 6 of 12. Raw agreement (accuracy) is 0.5.
The difference row shows direction. Five of six disagreements are the LLM grading one step higher; only q3d4 is graded lower. Every disagreement is off by exactly one grade.
Mean grade: human 1.5, LLM 1.83. Mean absolute error 0.5. A lenient judge inflates absolute metric values even if it orders documents well.

blocks.md: A **confusion matrix** counts pairs by (human grade, LLM grade). Row = human, column = LLM. The diagonal holds agreements; cells above the diagonal are pairs where the LLM was more generous. UMBRELA and the TREC 2024 RAG study publish exactly this view for real data.

scenes.caption: Observed counts. Each row sums to 3 (the human used each grade three times). Column sums are 1, 4, 3, 4: the LLM rarely says 0.
The diagonal: 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 6 agreements out of 12, so observed agreement p_o = 0.5.
Above the diagonal: 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 pairs graded higher by the LLM. Below: only 1. That asymmetry is leniency, the same direction NIST found for UMBRELA.

Expected counts if the two labellers were independent but kept their own grade frequencies: row total x column total / 12. The diagonal now sums to 0.25 + 1 + 0.75 + 1 = 3, so chance agreement p_e = 3/12 = 0.25.

blocks.caption: Cohen's kappa (as defined in the scikit-learn documentation): observed agreement minus chance agreement, divided by the most that could be gained over chance. Each labeller keeps its own grade frequencies when estimating chance.

blocks.title: Cohen's kappa for the toy, step by step
blocks.code:
H = [3,1,0,2, 2,0,1,3, 1,0,2,3]   # human grades
L = [3,2,0,2, 3,1,1,3, 1,1,3,2]   # LLM grades
n = len(H)
p_o = sum(h == l for h, l in zip(H, L)) / n
p_e = 0.0
for c in range(4):
    p_h = H.count(c) / n     # human uses grade c
    p_l = L.count(c) / n     # LLM uses grade c
    p_e += p_h * p_l         # both pick c by chance
kappa = (p_o - p_e) / (1 - p_e)

scenes.caption: Twelve pairs.
Observed agreement: 6 exact matches out of 12.
Grade 0: human 3/12, LLM 1/12. Chance both say 0: 3/144.
Grade 1: human 3/12, LLM 4/12, adds 12/144.
Grade 2: human 3/12, LLM 3/12, adds 9/144.
Grade 3: human 3/12, LLM 4/12, adds 12/144. Total chance agreement 36/144 = 0.25.
Kappa = (0.5 - 0.25) / (1 - 0.25) = 0.333. Half the pairs agree, but only a third of the possible improvement over chance is realised.

blocks.prompt: Suppose 90 of 100 pairs are non-relevant by human judgment (typical: TREC Robust 2004 had 293,998 non-relevant qrels against 17,412 relevant or highly relevant). A lazy judge outputs "non-relevant" for every pair. What are its accuracy and kappa?
blocks.reveal: Accuracy 0.9, kappa **0**. The judge uses one grade only, so $p_{\text{LLM}}(\text{nonrel}) = 1$ and $p_e = 0.9 \times 1 + 0.1 \times 0 = 0.9$, giving $\kappa = (0.9 - 0.9)/(1 - 0.9) = 0$. With skewed labels raw accuracy rewards guessing the majority grade; kappa does not. This is why Bing and TREC samples are stratified by grade and why papers report kappa, not accuracy.

scenes.caption: Kappa is a straight line in p_o that hits 0 at p_o = p_e and 1 at p_o = 1. Our 4-grade toy: p_e = 0.25, p_o = 0.5, kappa 0.333.
Binarised toy (0-1 vs 2-3): p_e = 0.5, p_o = 11/12 = 0.917, kappa 0.833. Merging grades raises both agreement and chance agreement.
Skewed collection, p_e = 0.9: an observed agreement of 0.9 is worth nothing. Slide p_e and watch the zero point move.

blocks.md: Unweighted kappa treats a 0 versus 3 disagreement the same as a 2 versus 3 one. For ordinal grades, **weighted kappa** charges disagreements by distance (scikit-learn: `weights='linear'` or `'quadratic'`):

blocks.caption: O is the observed confusion matrix, E the expected matrix from the marginals (scene 4 above). Toy: observed weighted disagreement 6/12 = 0.5, expected 2.333, so quadratic kappa = 1 - 0.5/2.333 = 0.786.

blocks.md: **Krippendorff's alpha** is the other standard: $\alpha = 1 - D_o/D_e$, observed over expected disagreement. It differs from kappa in two ways that matter in practice. It estimates chance from the **pooled** grades of all coders (not one distribution per coder), and it handles any number of coders, missing labels and nominal, ordinal or interval distance metrics. That suits relevance pools where each pair gets one, two or three human labels.

scenes.caption: Exact-match statistics: accuracy 0.5, Cohen's kappa 0.333, Krippendorff's alpha (nominal) 0.352. Alpha is slightly higher because it pools both coders' grades to estimate chance.
Distance-aware statistics: every toy disagreement is one grade apart, so linear (0.586) and quadratic (0.786) kappa, and interval alpha (0.790), are much higher.
Binarised at grade 2 (TREC DL convention), only one pair crosses the line: q1d2 (human 1, LLM 2). 11 of 12 agree, kappa 0.833. Coarser scales hide disagreement.

blocks.md: Always say which agreement number you report. UMBRELA's GPT-4o labels on TREC DL 2019 to 2023 had 4-grade kappa 0.31 to 0.37 but binarised kappa 0.42 to 0.50 on the same labels. A paper quoting one and a dashboard quoting the other are not comparable.

blocks.question: Two judges both reach 80% exact agreement with humans. Judge X is evaluated on a set that is 50% relevant; judge Y on a set that is 95% non-relevant, and Y says non-relevant to almost everything. Which statement is right?
options: They are equally good because accuracy is equal
Y is better because its set is harder
Kappa will be much lower for Y, because its chance agreement is high
Kappa cannot be computed on unbalanced sets
blocks.explain: Kappa subtracts the agreement expected from each labeller's grade frequencies. When both mostly say non-relevant, chance agreement is around 0.8, so 80% observed agreement is at or below chance and kappa is near zero or negative. That is why stratified samples and kappa are reported, not raw accuracy.

blocks.question: In the toy, every disagreement is exactly one grade apart. Which statistic best reflects that the judge is never wildly wrong?
options: Quadratic-weighted kappa or interval alpha
Unweighted Cohen's kappa
Raw accuracy
The number of pairs
blocks.explain: Weighted kappa and interval alpha charge disagreements by squared distance, so many off-by-one errors cost little (0.786 and 0.790 here) while unweighted kappa treats them as full misses (0.333). Report both: the unweighted one tells you how often grades match exactly.

lessons.title: From labels to leaderboards: do system rankings survive?

blocks.md:
Labels are a means. What a team acts on is the **ordering of systems**: which ranker ships. Thomas et al., UMBRELA and the TREC 2024 RAG study all ask the same question: if we score every system with LLM labels instead of human labels, do we get the same leaderboard?

Our toy has five rankers, A to E. Each returns its top 3 of the 4 candidates per query. We score each with NDCG@3 using gain = grade and discount $1/\log_2(1+i)$, then average over the 3 queries.

A worked case: for q2, system B returns q2d1, q2d4, q2d2. The human grades for q2's four documents are 2, 0, 1, 3 (d1 to d4) and the LLM's are 3, 1, 1, 3. The same ranked list gets a different NDCG under each set of labels, because both the gains and the ideal ordering change.

blocks.title: NDCG@3 for system B on q2, two label sets

scenes.caption: Human grades: DCG = 2 + 1.893 + 0 = 3.893. The ideal top 3 for q2 is grades 3, 2, 1, with IDCG = 3 + 1.262 + 0.5 = 4.762. NDCG@3 = 0.817.
LLM grades: q2d1 becomes 3 and q2d2 becomes 1. DCG = 3 + 1.893 + 0.5 = 5.393, and the LLM's ideal list is also 3, 3, 1, so NDCG@3 = 1.0.
Two one-grade disagreements turned B's q2 result from 0.817 into a perfect 1.0. Per-query scores move a lot; the question is whether averages over queries still order systems correctly.
Human labels: A 1.000, C 0.921, B 0.886, D 0.842, E 0.457. Order A, C, B, D, E.

LLM labels: B 0.991, A 0.974, C 0.951, D 0.916, E 0.601. Leniency lifts most scores, most for the weak system E (0.457 to 0.601). A falls from 1.000 to 0.974 because its q3 list is no longer ideal under LLM grades.
Order under LLM labels: B, A, C, D, E. B jumped from third to first; the bottom of the table is unchanged.

blocks.caption: Kendall's tau over m systems: C concordant pairs (both label sets order the two systems the same way), D discordant pairs. With no ties this is tau-a; scipy's default tau-b also adjusts for ties.

blocks.title: Kendall's tau over the 10 system pairs

scenes.caption: Five systems give 5 x 4 / 2 = 10 pairs. For each pair, which system wins under each label set?
8 pairs agree (concordant), 2 disagree: A versus B and B versus C. Both involve B, which gains a lot from the LLM's leniency on q2d1 (its q2 NDCG rises from 0.817 to 1.0).
tau = (8 - 2) / 10 = 0.6. One B jump costs 0.4 of tau with only five systems; with 77 runs a single swap would barely register.

blocks.prompt: Our toy leaderboard has tau 0.6. Real studies with dozens of systems report run-level tau between about 0.77 and 0.94. Would you ship based on the LLM leaderboard if your top two candidates differ by a small margin?
blocks.reveal: Not on that alone. A high overall tau is dominated by easy pairs (strong versus weak systems). Clarke and Dietz re-examined TREC 2024 RAG: overall tau 0.89, but **0.51 among the top 20 runs** and 0.56 among the top 15; the run ranked first by UMBRELA placed fifth under human labels. Close calls at the top are exactly where the judge is least reliable, so they need human labels or a significance test.

blocks.md:
What the primary studies found at system level:

- **Bing on TREC Robust 2004** (110 runs, GPT-4, prompt -DNA-): tau from 0.77 (MAP@100) to 0.86 depending on the metric. Top three runs identical under all metrics.
- **Faggioli et al.** (GPT-3.5, TREC DL 2021): tau 0.86 on NDCG@10, but binarised kappa only 0.26; the top run stayed on top.
- **UMBRELA** (GPT-4o, TREC DL 2019 to 2023, NDCG@10): tau 0.87 to 0.94.
- **TREC 2024 RAG** (77 runs, 27 fully human-judged topics): run-level tau 0.890 for nDCG@20, 0.944 for nDCG@100, 0.929 for Recall@100, but only 0.553 when tau is computed per topic and averaged.

Label-level agreement can be modest (kappa 0.3 to 0.6) while system-level agreement is high (tau near 0.9), because errors that are not systematic average out over many queries. The reverse also holds: a small systematic bias can flip close systems even when kappa looks fine.

blocks.question: In our toy, which change would most likely raise Kendall's tau between the human and LLM leaderboards, without changing the judge?
options: Using fewer queries
Using many more queries, so per-query label noise averages out
Reporting accuracy instead of tau
Removing the weakest system E
blocks.explain: System scores are averages over queries. Random label errors shrink in the average as queries are added (the TREC RAG Monte Carlo shows tau dropping from 0.890 to 0.768 when only a third of topics are used).

blocks.question: Per-topic tau in the TREC 2024 RAG study (0.553 for nDCG@20) is much lower than run-level tau (0.890). What does that tell you?
options: The LLM labels are useless
Run-level averages are wrong
LLM labels are noisy for any single query, so per-query diagnosis needs more care than leaderboard ranking
Per-topic tau is always lower because of a formula error
blocks.explain: Within one topic, label disagreements reorder runs a lot; averaged over 27 topics the noise cancels. Use LLM labels confidently for aggregate comparisons, cautiously for statements about a single query.

lessons.title: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference

blocks.md:
Pointwise grading (one passage, one grade) is not the only mode. Search teams also ask a judge **pairwise** questions: "for this query, is result A or result B better?" Pairwise preferences are often easier to give than absolute grades, and Bing's gold set is itself made of about 2.5 million preferred versus non-preferred result pairs, scored by pairwise accuracy.

Zheng et al. (2023), who introduced MT-Bench and studied LLM-as-a-judge for chat answers, catalogued the biases that pairwise judges show. They carry over to any setting where the judge compares two texts.

- **Position bias**: preferring an answer because of where it appears (first or second) in the prompt.
- **Verbosity bias**: preferring the longer answer even when the extra length adds nothing.
- **Self-enhancement bias**: preferring answers produced by the judge model itself.

To measure position bias, Zheng et al. asked each judge to compare two similar answers, then swapped their order. **Consistency** is the fraction of cases where the verdict is the same after the swap.

blocks.title: Pairwise judge biases in MT-Bench (Zheng et al.)

scenes.caption: Consistency after swapping the order of two similar answers (default prompt). Even the best judge, GPT-4, gave the same verdict both ways only 65% of the time.
Share of cases where the judge favoured whichever answer came first. Claude-v1 picked the first answer 75% of the time.
"Repetitive list" attack: pad an answer with a rephrased copy of its own list. Failure = the padded answer wins. 91.3% for Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5, 8.7% for GPT-4 (23 answers).

blocks.md: Zheng et al.'s conservative fix for position bias: **call the judge twice with the order swapped and declare a win only if both orders agree; otherwise call it a tie.** It doubles the cost and turns inconsistency into visible ties instead of hidden noise. Few-shot examples raised GPT-4's consistency from 65.0% to 77.5%, but made prompts about 4 times as expensive and the authors note consistency is not the same as accuracy.

blocks.title: Swap-and-tie for a pairwise relevance judgment

scenes.caption: Pair 1, first call: document A shown first, B second.
Second call with the order swapped. The judge now prefers whatever is in first place, B.
The verdicts disagree, so the harness records a tie. A naive single call would have recorded a win for A on position alone.
Pair 2: both orders prefer C. Only consistent verdicts count as wins.

blocks.md: **Self-enhancement** is the hardest to prove. In MT-Bench, compared with humans, GPT-4 gave itself about a 10% higher win rate and Claude-v1 about 25% higher, but GPT-3.5 did not favour itself, and the authors state their data could not determine whether self-enhancement bias exists. For relevance labels the analogous worry is that a judge prefers passages that look like LLM-written text, or rankings produced by an LLM. Clarke and Dietz cite later work (Balog et al.) reporting "a clear and substantial bias in favor of LLM-based rankers".

Despite the biases, agreement can be high where it counts: on MT-Bench, GPT-4's pairwise verdicts agreed with human experts 85% of the time on non-tied votes, versus 81% between humans. Bias and good average agreement coexist; the biases show up on specific slices (similar answers, long answers, same-family outputs).

For pointwise relevance grades the order bias has an analogue: grading many passages in one prompt lets earlier passages anchor later ones. Grade one passage per call, as the Bing and UMBRELA prompts do, or randomise and repeat if you batch.

blocks.question: Your pairwise judge compares old ranker versus new ranker results and always shows the new ranker's result first. It reports a 58% win rate for the new ranker. What should you do first?
options: Ship the new ranker, 58% is a clear win
Rerun every comparison with the order swapped and count a win only when both orders agree; inconsistent pairs become ties
Switch to a longer prompt so the judge reads more carefully
Ask the judge to explain its reasoning and trust the explanation
blocks.explain: With a fixed order, position bias is confounded with the treatment. Swap-and-tie (Zheng et al.) removes the position effect: wins must survive both orders. Randomising the order per pair is the cheaper large-scale alternative.

blocks.question: A colleague adds an "include more detail" step to the generator in a RAG system, and the LLM judge's preference for its answers rises from 50% to 70%. Which explanation should you rule out before celebrating?
options: Verbosity bias: the judge may be rewarding length rather than better content
Position bias in the generator
Kendall's tau is too low
The gold set is too large
blocks.explain: Zheng et al.'s repetitive list attack shows weaker judges preferring padded answers over 90% of the time. Check with length-controlled comparisons or human spot checks before attributing the gain to quality.

lessons.title: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely

blocks.md:
Faggioli et al. raised a deeper problem than bias: **circularity**. An LLM that can judge relevance can also be used to rank. If the same model and prompt that produce the labels are also inside a system, the evaluation rewards the system for agreeing with the judge, not with people.

Soboroff, quoted by Clarke and Dietz, puts it bluntly: retrieval and evaluation are the same problem. A relevance judge is a pointwise reranker by another name.

blocks.title: How a judge becomes part of the system it judges

nodes.label:
Same LLM judge
labels the pool

scenes.caption: Build F by taking weak system E's candidates and sorting them by the LLM judge's grades (ties keep E's order).
Now evaluate F with labels from the same judge. The ranking was built from the answer key.
Humans only checked the judge on a gold sample; they never see that F's top results are exactly the judge's favourites.

blocks.title: The toy leaderboard with circular system F

scenes.caption: Under LLM labels F scores a perfect 1.000 on every query and tops the table: F, B, A, C, D, E.
Under human labels F scores 0.904: genuinely better than E (0.457), but third, behind A (1.000) and C (0.921). Order A, C, F, B, D, E.
With F added, 11 of 15 system pairs agree and 4 disagree, so tau drops from 0.6 to (11 - 4)/15 = 0.467. The new disagreements all involve the circular system.

blocks.md:
This is not hypothetical. In TREC 2024 RAG, team WaterlooClarke submitted run **uwc1**, deliberately built by pooling 15 preliminary runs and ordering passages with GPT-4o relevance and preference judgments. It ranked **5th under UMBRELA labels but 28th under human labels**.

Clarke and Dietz then simulated every TREC 2024 RAG run being reranked with the track's own UMBRELA labels. Reranking genuinely improved the runs under human judgments, but evaluating those reranked runs with the same UMBRELA labels broke the leaderboard: twelve systems scored NDCG above 0.95 under UMBRELA while scoring only 0.68 to 0.72 under human labels.

blocks.title: Kendall's tau, UMBRELA vs human, TREC 2024 RAG (Clarke and Dietz)

scenes.caption: Submitted runs as they were: tau 0.85 among the top 60, but 0.51 among the top 20 and 0.56 among the top 15. Agreement is weakest where decisions are made.
Every run reranked with UMBRELA, then judged by UMBRELA: tau falls to 0.63, 0.44 and 0.49 (and to -0.40 among the top 5).

blocks.md: Goodhart's law, which Clarke and Dietz quote, is the general form: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Thomas et al. flag the same risks from the industry side: optimising toward LLM labels may overfit to the LLM's idiosyncrasies, LLM labels may favour rankers that themselves use LLMs, and web authors may start optimising for LLM judges.

A practical checklist assembled from these sources:

1. **Build a gold set** from the people the system serves (first-party feedback if you can), stratified by grade and slice. Report kappa (and weighted kappa) and the confusion matrix, not raw accuracy.
2. **Tune the prompt on half the gold set, check on the other half**; re-validate on every model or prompt change.
3. **Validate at the decision level**: Kendall's tau on system rankings, and especially agreement among the top systems you are choosing between.
4. **Separate judge and ranker**: different model or prompt, and a held-out judge the system cannot see or train on.
5. **Audit continuously**: Bing re-labels a stratified weekly sample with trained assessors and tracks a fixed query set that should not change day to day.
6. **Keep humans for close calls** at the top of the leaderboard and for new test collections meant for reuse.

Use an LLM judge to label at scale, but never let the measurement and the thing measured share the same model and prompt, and keep a human gold set to check the instrument. When the judge is also a ranking component, its scores stop measuring anything.

blocks.question: Your team's reranker is a fine-tuned copy of the same LLM and prompt used to label your offline test set. Offline NDCG@10 jumps from 0.71 to 0.93. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Ship it: a 0.22 gain is far outside noise
Re-evaluate with labels from humans or a judge independent of the reranker, at least on a sample and on the top competing systems
Report the gain with quadratic-weighted kappa instead
Raise the judge temperature to reduce bias
blocks.explain: This is the circular setup Faggioli et al. warned about and Clarke and Dietz demonstrated: scores near the ceiling under the judge's own labels while human-labelled NDCG barely moves. Only an independent reference can tell whether the gain is real.

blocks.question: In the TREC 2024 RAG study, overall run-level tau between UMBRELA and human labels was 0.89. Why do Clarke and Dietz still argue against replacing human assessment?
options: Because 0.89 is below chance
Because kappa was not reported
Because LLMs cannot output integers reliably
Because agreement collapses among the top runs, a deliberately LLM-reranked run jumped from 28th to 5th, and reranking with the judge makes the evaluation circular
blocks.explain: Overall tau is dominated by easy comparisons. Among the top 20 runs tau was 0.51, run uwc1 showed the metric can be gamed, and the circularity simulation drove tau down to 0.63 among the top 60 and negative among the top 5.

blocks.question: Which practice from Bing's deployment directly guards against the judge drifting silently after a model update?
options: Using a role statement in the prompt
Simulating five judges per call
Weekly re-labelling of a stratified sample of recent LLM labels by trained assessors, plus a fixed query set expected not to change
Binarising grades before computing kappa
blocks.explain: Thomas et al. describe weekly stratified human re-labelling with monitoring of disagreement rates and patterns, and a large set of queries consistently re-labelled to detect any change. The other options are prompt choices, not monitoring.
